Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Graphic Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Intrusive Thoughts: Unwanted thoughts, Visual (Injuries): Visible injuries or wounds on others, Authority Presence: Police
  Maladaptive Strategies: Screen Escape: I spend long hours on my phone, games, or internet to avoid thinking, Avoid People: avoid other people, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Escape Route Planning: I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it

Vignette:
Mark is a 46-year-old graphic designer who lives with his wife in a quiet suburban neighborhood. Two years ago, he was stopped at a red light on his way home from a late client meeting when he saw a confrontation unfolding on the sidewalk between two police officers and a young man. Mark watched the man raise his hands, then saw an officer shove him to the ground, and then—he still cannot fully describe it when he tries—the other officer struck the man repeatedly with a baton while he was on the ground. Mark was still staring, frozen, when a third officer appeared at his car window, banging on the glass, ordering him to move along. He drove away shaking, the image of the man’s split-open forehead and the blood on the concrete lodged in his mind like a shard. He never learned the man’s name. He never saw a news story. He called the police department the next day and was told there was no record of any incident at that location. When he tried to describe it to his wife that night, he lost the thread halfway through, his voice going flat, his hands curling into fists. He could not finish.

In the weeks that followed, Mark could not relax. Even in his own home—a place he had always thought of as safe—he found himself scanning the room for exit routes before he could sit down. He began to check the back door twice before bed, and he had to stop himself from calculating how fast he could reach the sliding glass door from the sofa. At the grocery store, he would walk the perimeter first, locating every emergency exit, then choose a spot with clear sightlines to the door. His body stayed tensed, his shoulders pressed up toward his ears, his jaw locked. He told himself he was just being careful. But he knew, deep down, that he was waiting for something bad to happen again.

The memories returned without warning. A siren in the distance. A blue uniform in the corner of his eye at a coffee shop. A customer walking in with a bandage across his cheek. Each time, the full scene would hit him—the sound of the baton, the wet crack, the officer’s voice yelling at him through the window—and he would feel such a wave of emotion that he had to physically stop walking, or put down whatever he was holding, and breathe until it passed. He could not predict when it would happen, and that made everything feel dangerous.

He started to avoid people entirely. If a neighbor waved from the driveway, he would pretend not to see him and head back inside. He told his wife he was just tired, swamped with work. And he was. At his desk, he found himself unable to tolerate a single moment of silence in his own mind. He kept his earbuds in all day, cycling through music, podcasts, and videos. As soon as he finished a task, he pulled out his phone and scrolled through games or social media, sometimes for hours, until his wife called him to dinner. The phone became a refuge: as long as his attention was occupied, the images could not break through. But the price was that he never fully engaged with anything else. He stopped answering calls from old friends. He let his side projects slide. His wife complained that he was always "there but not there," and he could not argue with her.

He became obsessed with the injustice of it all. The officers were still working. No one had been held accountable. The thought would loop in his head at night: *Nothing has been done. Nothing.* And with that came a deeper sense that his life had been destroyed—not just that night, but in everything that followed. The things that used to matter—designing a good logo, taking his wife out on a Saturday, laughing with a colleague—felt hollow. Nothing felt meaningful anymore. He could not say exactly what he was supposed to be working toward.

It was his wife who finally scheduled the appointment. She told him, gently, that he was not the man she married. He had been hoping it would fade on its own. Instead, the hypervigilance had only sharpened, the avoidance had narrowed his world to the length of an iPhone screen, and the memories were coming more often now, not less. When the clinician asked him what he wanted most from treatment, Mark paused for a long time. Then he said, quietly, that he wanted to be able to sit in a room—any room—without scanning for the exits. He wanted to stop feeling like the moment he looked away, something terrible would happen again. And underneath that, what he did not say aloud, was that he wanted to find some way to believe that his life still had a shape, a direction, a reason.
